<jats:p><span>Procedural Content Generation (PCG) provides a means of automatically&nbsp;</span><span>generating diverse, complex functional environments for video game playing&nbsp;</span><span>agents. While various optimization approaches have been used to generate&nbsp;</span><span>content meeting computable functional constraints, more open-ended human priors&nbsp;</span><span>and directives are difficult to bake in to such methods. We propose Agentic&nbsp;</span><span>Procedural Content Generation, a paradigm in which tool-calling large language&nbsp;</span><span>models generate video game levels that are both functional and steerable via&nbsp;</span><span>natural language. Equipped with local brushes, generative algorithms, and&nbsp;</span><span>evaluation functions, agents iteratively refine content toward specified design&nbsp;</span><span>objectives. We show that the framework applies to both static level design&nbsp;</span><span>tasks and environments with dynamic gameplay mechanics, while satisfying</span>
<br><span>intended functional constraints. Beyond such constraints, the same framework&nbsp;</span><span>can respond to open-ended gameplay prompts and produce levels with stronger&nbsp;</span><span>structural and stylistic coherence than purely metric-driven search, suggesting&nbsp;</span><span>that Agentic PCG is a framework for balancing functional constraint&nbsp;</span><span>satisfaction with free-form design control.</span></jats:p>
title: Agentic PCG: Procedural Content Generation via Tool-using LLMs

items.abstract: <jats:p>This project presents an Agentic AI system for autonomous code quality diagnosis, behavior-preserving refactoring, and empirical comparison of multiple machine learning and AI-based agents. The system moves beyond traditional static analysis tools by implementing a self-healing software engineering pipeline that scans Python repositories, extracts code quality metrics, detects code smells and clone patterns, retrieves public software engineering knowledge using Retrieval-Augmented Generation, applies safe refactoring actions, validates modified code through automated tests, and compares the outcomes of multiple independent agents. The implemented system evaluates four agents: a deterministic Rule-Based Agent, a Retrieval-Augmented Generation Agent using public software engineering knowledge and Tavily search, a Groq-powered Large Language Model Agent, and a tabular Q-Learning Agent. Each agent is executed on a safe copy of the same repository, and the final output is selected only after before-and-after metric comparison and test validation. Experiments are performed on public GitHub repositories including GildedRose, ExpenseReport-Refactoring-Kata, Theatrical-Players-Refactoring-Kata, and Dependency-Breaking-Katas. The final system also includes a Streamlit application where users can directly enter Groq and Tavily API keys, run comparative analysis, visualize metric changes, and generate reports. The updated comparison ensures that different agents produce different metric improvements, making the evaluation more realistic and suitable for an Applied Machine Learning final project.</jats:p>
title: Agentic AI for Code Quality: A Four-Agent Machine Learning System for Repository Refactoring, Public RAG, Groq Reasoning, and Reinforcement Learning

items.abstract: Background: Software repositories continuously accumulate technical debt in the form of code smells, duplicated logic, high complexity, and poor maintainability. Although static analysis tools can identify these issues, they typically stop at diagnosis and do not autonomously perform behavior-preserving repairs or compare multiple repair strategies. Objective: This work presents an Agentic AI framework for autonomous code quality improvement that integrates multiple artificial intelligence approaches to detect, analyze, refactor, and validate software repositories while preserving functional correctness. Methods: The proposed system implements four complementary agents: (i) a deterministic Rule-Based Agent, (ii) a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) Agent using public software engineering knowledge and Tavily search, (iii) a Groq-powered Large Language Model Agent for semantic reasoning, and (iv) a Q-Learning Agent for adaptive refactoring policy selection. Python repositories are analyzed using Abstract Syntax Tree (AST)-based static analysis to extract maintainability metrics, detect code smells and clone patterns, and compute repository-level quality indicators. Each agent independently performs refactoring on isolated repository copies, followed by automated syntax checking, test validation, and metric-based evaluation. A Supervisor Agent compares all candidate solutions and selects the best validated outcome. Results: The framework was evaluated on four publicly available GitHub repositories: GildedRose, ExpenseReport Refactoring Kata, Theatrical Players Refactoring Kata, and Dependency Breaking Katas. Experimental results demonstrated measurable improvements in repository quality, including quality score gains of up to 64.44% , issue reductions of up to 66.67% , and risk reductions approaching 40% , while preserving software behavior through automated validation. Comparative evaluation further showed that different AI agents exhibit distinct strengths depending on repository characteristics, with Rule-Based, RAG, LLM, and Reinforcement Learning approaches outperforming one another under different software maintenance scenarios. Conclusion: The proposed multi-agent architecture demonstrates that combining static analysis, Retrieval-Augmented Generation, large language models, reinforcement learning, and automated validation enables a practical self-healing software engineering pipeline. The framework advances autonomous software maintenance by moving beyond issue detection toward intelligent diagnosis, safe behavior-preserving refactoring, empirical agent comparison, and production-oriented code quality improvement.
title: Agentic AI for Code Quality: A Four-Agent Machine Learning System for Repository Refactoring, Public RAG, Groq Reasoning, and Reinforcement Learning
